problems.title: Employees and their managers
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: The org directory behind a Microsoft Teams-style chat app keeps one row per employee, and each row points at the `emp_id` of that person's manager. Return every employee as `emp_id`, `employee` (their name) and `manager` (their manager's name). Everyone must appear, including the person nobody reports to, whose `manager` is NULL. Order by `emp_id`.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee. `manager_id` points at another row of this table and is NULL for the top of the company.

hints_md: The same table plays two roles in this question: the employee and the manager. Think about how to refer to it twice in one query.
Count the rows in your result. Does it have as many rows as the table has employees?
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Self-join, used whenever a row refers to another row of the same table (manager, parent, referrer). An interviewer reaches for it on org charts and category trees.

**Shape:** read the table twice under different aliases, one standing for the employee and one for the manager, and connect the employee's pointer column to the manager's key. Decide what happens to rows that have no partner.

**Syntax:** a table alias such as `FROM employees AS e` gives each copy its own name; without distinct aliases the column names are ambiguous. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row from the left side and fills the right side's columns with NULL when nothing matches.

**Trap:** an inner join quietly drops the top of the hierarchy because its pointer is NULL and NULL never equals anything. Also easy to get backwards: which side's key is compared to which side's pointer.

**Interview follow-up:** how would you list each manager with the number of people who report to them directly?

solutions.label: LEFT self-join
solutions.explain_md: Both aliases read the same table. The employee's `manager_id` is matched to the manager's `emp_id`; LEFT JOIN keeps the employee with a NULL pointer and gives a NULL manager name.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

solutions.label: Correlated subquery
solutions.explain_md: Looks up the manager's name per employee; no match (NULL pointer) yields NULL, so the top person is kept without any join.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name AS employee,
       (SELECT m.name FROM employees m WHERE m.emp_id = e.manager_id) AS manager
FROM employees e
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

traps.explain_md: An inner join drops the employee whose `manager_id` is NULL, because NULL = anything is never true. The CEO disappears.
traps.sql:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

traps.explain_md: The comparison is reversed: it pairs each person with someone whose pointer targets them, i.e. a person with their reports, so the names in `manager` are the wrong people.
traps.sql:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.manager_id = e.emp_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id, m.emp_id;

problems.title: Teammates who joined the same year
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: An online game studio wants to send a veteran badge to pairs of guildmates who created their accounts in the same calendar year. Return one row per pair as `guild`, `handle_a` and `handle_b`, where `handle_a` is the player with the smaller `player_id`. A pair must appear once, never twice in swapped order, and nobody is paired with themselves. Order by `guild`, then the two ids.

tables.name: players
tables.description_md: One row per player account; each player belongs to one guild.

hints_md: You need to compare every player with every other player. Which conditions say 'same guild' and 'same year'?
A pair (BlitzBee, DuskRunner) and the pair (DuskRunner, BlitzBee) describe the same two people. What condition on the ids keeps only one of them and also removes (BlitzBee, BlitzBee)?
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Self-join that builds unordered pairs. Interviewers use it for 'find pairs of rows that share an attribute'.

**Shape:** read the table twice, match the shared attributes with equality, and add one extra condition on the ids so each pair is produced in one orientation only.

**Syntax:** `YEAR(date_col)` returns the calendar year as a number. A strict inequality between the two ids (`<`) removes self-pairs and mirrored duplicates in one step; `<>` only removes self-pairs.

**Trap:** forgetting the id condition gives people paired with themselves and every pair twice; `<>` alone still doubles every pair.

**Interview follow-up:** how would you count, per guild, how many such pairs exist without listing them?

solutions.label: Self-join with a.player_id < b.player_id
solutions.explain_md: Equality on guild and creation year finds the pairs; the strict id inequality keeps exactly one orientation of each pair and removes self-pairs.
solutions.sql:
SELECT a.guild, a.handle AS handle_a, b.handle AS handle_b
FROM players a
JOIN players b
  ON a.guild = b.guild
 AND YEAR(a.created_on) = YEAR(b.created_on)
 AND a.player_id < b.player_id
ORDER BY a.guild, a.player_id, b.player_id;

traps.explain_md: With no id condition every player is paired with themselves and every real pair appears in both orders.
traps.sql:
SELECT a.guild, a.handle AS handle_a, b.handle AS handle_b
FROM players a
JOIN players b
  ON a.guild = b.guild
 AND YEAR(a.created_on) = YEAR(b.created_on)
ORDER BY a.guild, a.player_id, b.player_id;

traps.explain_md: `<>` removes self-pairs but keeps both (BlitzBee, DuskRunner) and (DuskRunner, BlitzBee), so each pair is doubled.
traps.sql:
SELECT a.guild, a.handle AS handle_a, b.handle AS handle_b
FROM players a
JOIN players b
  ON a.guild = b.guild
 AND YEAR(a.created_on) = YEAR(b.created_on)
 AND a.player_id <> b.player_id
ORDER BY a.guild, a.player_id, b.player_id;

problems.title: Streams up on the day before
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: A Spotify-style analytics table logs total daily streams for a new single, but the ingestion job failed on a few days, so some dates are missing. Return the days with strictly more streams than the previous calendar day, as `stream_date`, `streams` and `prev_streams` (the previous calendar day's count). A day whose previous calendar day has no row must not be compared with anything. Order by `stream_date`.

tables.name: daily_streams
tables.description_md: One row per day with data; some dates are absent.

hints_md: Look at the dates: 2025-03-05 and 2025-03-11 are missing. What should happen to the rows of 2025-03-06 and 2025-03-12?
'The previous row' and 'the previous calendar day' are not the same thing when days are missing.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Period-over-period comparison on a table that may have gaps. A self-join on a date offset is the robust form; interviewers like it because it does not silently trust row order.

**Shape:** pair each day with the row whose date is exactly one day earlier; only days that find such a partner can be compared. Then filter on the counts.

**Syntax:** `date_col - INTERVAL 1 DAY` shifts a date back by one day; `DATEDIFF(later, earlier)` returns the number of days between two dates as an integer.

**Trap:** comparing with the previous row (for example via a window function) instead of the previous date: across a gap it compares days that are not adjacent.

**Interview follow-up:** how would you solve it with LAG, and what extra check does it need?

solutions.label: Self-join on the previous date
solutions.explain_md: Joining on the exact previous calendar date means a day with no partner (after a gap) simply has no row to compare, and the stream filter finishes the job.
solutions.sql:
SELECT t.stream_date, t.streams, p.streams AS prev_streams
FROM daily_streams t
JOIN daily_streams p ON p.stream_date = t.stream_date - INTERVAL 1 DAY
WHERE t.streams > p.streams
ORDER BY t.stream_date;

solutions.label: LAG with a date check
solutions.explain_md: LAG fetches the previous row's date and count; the DATEDIFF test rejects previous rows that are not exactly one day earlier.
solutions.sql:
SELECT stream_date, streams, prev_streams
FROM (
  SELECT stream_date, streams,
         LAG(stream_date) OVER (ORDER BY stream_date) AS prev_date,
         LAG(streams) OVER (ORDER BY stream_date) AS prev_streams
  FROM daily_streams
) x
WHERE DATEDIFF(stream_date, prev_date) = 1
  AND streams > prev_streams
ORDER BY stream_date;

traps.explain_md: Using the previous row regardless of its date treats 2025-03-06 as higher than 'yesterday' although 2025-03-05 has no row, and does the same for 2025-03-12.
traps.sql:
SELECT stream_date, streams, prev_streams
FROM (
  SELECT stream_date, streams,
         LAG(streams) OVER (ORDER BY stream_date) AS prev_streams
  FROM daily_streams
) x
WHERE streams > prev_streams
ORDER BY stream_date;

traps.explain_md: The date offset points the wrong way: each day is compared with the next day, so the result answers 'more than tomorrow'.
traps.sql:
SELECT t.stream_date, t.streams, p.streams AS prev_streams
FROM daily_streams t
JOIN daily_streams p ON p.stream_date = t.stream_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY
WHERE t.streams > p.streams
ORDER BY t.stream_date;

problems.title: Titles nobody has watched
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: The content team at a Netflix-like streaming company wants to review catalogue titles that no profile has ever started. Return the `title_id` and `title` of every title that does not appear in the watch history, ordered by `title_id`.

tables.name: watch_history
tables.description_md: One row per viewing session of a title by a profile.

hints_md: You are looking for titles with no matching viewing sessions. Some titles appear many times in `watch_history`.
After combining the two tables so that unmatched titles are kept, what does an unmatched row look like on the watch-history side?
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Anti-join, 'rows in A with no match in B'. Interviewers ask it as 'customers who never ordered', 'titles never watched'.

**Shape:** either keep every title and look for the ones whose partner columns are empty, or ask for titles for which no matching session exists. Both express 'absence' without counting.

**Syntax:** `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL` keeps the unmatched left rows (test a column that can never be NULL in a real match, such as the key). `NOT EXISTS (subquery)` is true when the subquery returns no rows.

**Trap:** joining on `<>` does not mean 'has no match' - it pairs each title with every session of a different title.

**Interview follow-up:** is there a difference in result or performance between the LEFT JOIN and NOT EXISTS forms?

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN, keep the unmatched
solutions.explain_md: Every title is kept; those with no session get NULLs on the right, and the IS NULL test on the session key isolates them.
solutions.sql:
SELECT t.title_id, t.title
FROM titles t
LEFT JOIN watch_history w ON w.title_id = t.title_id
WHERE w.watch_id IS NULL
ORDER BY t.title_id;

solutions.label: NOT EXISTS
solutions.explain_md: States the rule directly: keep the title when no session refers to it.

traps.explain_md: A `<>` join matches each title with every session of another title, so almost every title shows up.
traps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t.title_id, t.title
FROM titles t
JOIN watch_history w ON w.title_id <> t.title_id
ORDER BY t.title_id;

traps.explain_md: The unmatched-row test is on a title column, which is never NULL after a LEFT JOIN from titles, so the filter removes everything.
traps.sql:
SELECT t.title_id, t.title
FROM titles t
LEFT JOIN watch_history w ON w.title_id = t.title_id
WHERE t.title IS NULL
ORDER BY t.title_id;

problems.title: Tweets from accounts you have not muted
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: A Twitter-style app lets users mute accounts, and the timeline must hide tweets from muted accounts. Return `tweet_id`, `author_handle` and `body` of the tweets whose author is not on the `mute_list`, ordered by `tweet_id`. A tweet from a deleted account has no author handle and cannot match any mute entry, so it is shown; one mute entry is a keyword mute and has no handle either.

tables.name: tweets
tables.description_md: One row per tweet. `author_handle` is NULL when the author account was deleted.

tables.name: mute_list
tables.description_md: Mute entries. `muted_handle` is NULL for a keyword mute.

hints_md: Check the `mute_list` table carefully, including its NULL row. How does a comparison against NULL behave?
Think about a form of 'no matching row exists' that does not compare a value to the whole list at once.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Anti-join over a list that may contain NULLs. Interviewers use this to see whether you know why NOT IN is risky.

**Shape:** keep a tweet when no mute entry carries the same handle. Express it as an existence test or by looking for the unmatched side of an outer join.

**Syntax:** `x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` evaluates to unknown for every x that is not a or b, so it never keeps the row. `NOT EXISTS (subquery)` only asks whether any row comes back, and a NULL never matches an equality.

**Trap:** `NOT IN (SELECT ...)` against a column containing a NULL returns an empty result.

**Interview follow-up:** can you make NOT IN safe, and which form would you prefer in production?

solutions.label: NOT EXISTS
solutions.explain_md: The correlated test only asks whether a mute entry with the same handle exists. A NULL handle matches nothing, so the deleted-account tweet is kept and the keyword-mute row is harmless.

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN, keep the unmatched
solutions.explain_md: Tweets whose author is not muted find no mute row, so the mute key is NULL for them.
solutions.sql:
SELECT t.tweet_id, t.author_handle, t.body
FROM tweets t
LEFT JOIN mute_list m ON m.muted_handle = t.author_handle
WHERE m.mute_id IS NULL
ORDER BY t.tweet_id;

solutions.label: NOT IN with the NULL removed
solutions.explain_md: NOT IN is safe once NULLs are removed from the list. A tweet with no author needs its own test, because comparing a NULL with a list never yields true.
solutions.sql:
SELECT t.tweet_id, t.author_handle, t.body
FROM tweets t
WHERE t.author_handle IS NULL
   OR t.author_handle NOT IN (SELECT muted_handle FROM mute_list WHERE muted_handle IS NOT NULL)
ORDER BY t.tweet_id;

traps.explain_md: The mute list contains a NULL handle, so `NOT IN` evaluates to unknown for every tweet and the query returns nothing.
traps.sql:
SELECT tweet_id, author_handle, body
FROM tweets
WHERE author_handle NOT IN (SELECT muted_handle FROM mute_list)
ORDER BY tweet_id;

traps.explain_md: A `<>` join pairs each tweet with every mute entry that differs, so muted authors' tweets appear too.
traps.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t.tweet_id, t.author_handle, t.body
FROM tweets t
JOIN mute_list m ON m.muted_handle <> t.author_handle
ORDER BY t.tweet_id;

problems.title: Cards with no recent transactions
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: Treat 2025-06-30 as today. A bank's fraud team wants a list of dormant cards: cards with no transaction on or after 2025-06-01, including cards that have never been used. Return `card_id` and `holder_name`, one row per card, ordered by `card_id`.
hints_md: A card that was used in January and again last week is still active. Does your result contain such a card?
The date test describes which transactions count as 'recent'. Where in the query should it live so that cards without any recent transaction are not lost?
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Anti-join with a condition on the other side. Interviewers use it for 'no activity in the last N days'.

**Shape:** the match is not just 'same card' but 'same card and a recent transaction'. Keep the cards for which that kind of match does not exist.

**Syntax:** in an outer join, a condition in `ON` decides what counts as a match, while the same condition in `WHERE` filters the rows afterwards (and turns the outer join into an inner one for that column). `NOT EXISTS` can carry the same extra condition inside its subquery.

**Trap:** filtering for old transactions instead of excluding recent ones: a card with an old and a recent transaction is wrongly returned, and cards with no transactions disappear or are repeated.

**Interview follow-up:** how would you report the date of each returned card's last transaction (NULL if none)?

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN with the date in ON
solutions.explain_md: Only transactions from 2025-06-01 on can match. A card with no such transaction gets NULLs and is kept by the IS NULL test, including cards that were never used.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.card_id, c.holder_name
FROM cards c
LEFT JOIN card_transactions t
  ON t.card_id = c.card_id
 AND t.txn_date >= '2025-06-01'
WHERE t.txn_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.card_id;

solutions.label: NOT EXISTS
solutions.explain_md: States it directly: no transaction for the card on or after the cutoff.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.card_id, c.holder_name
FROM cards c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM card_transactions t
  WHERE t.card_id = c.card_id AND t.txn_date >= '2025-06-01'
)
ORDER BY c.card_id;

solutions.label: Latest transaction per card
solutions.explain_md: Compute each card's most recent transaction and keep those with none or an old one.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.card_id, c.holder_name
FROM cards c
LEFT JOIN card_transactions t ON t.card_id = c.card_id
GROUP BY c.card_id, c.holder_name
HAVING MAX(t.txn_date) IS NULL OR MAX(t.txn_date) < '2025-06-01'
ORDER BY c.card_id;

traps.explain_md: Looking for old transactions returns cards that have one old transaction even when they were also used recently, and repeats a card once per old transaction.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.card_id, c.holder_name
FROM cards c
LEFT JOIN card_transactions t ON t.card_id = c.card_id
WHERE t.txn_date < '2025-06-01' OR t.txn_date IS NULL
ORDER BY c.card_id;

traps.explain_md: Excluding only cards that have never been used answers a different question; cards whose last transaction is old are missing.
traps.sql:
SELECT card_id, holder_name
FROM cards
WHERE card_id NOT IN (SELECT card_id FROM card_transactions)
ORDER BY card_id;

problems.title: Customers with a big order
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: On an Amazon-style marketplace, a big order is one with an order total of 500.00 or more. Return the `customer_id` and `name` of every customer who has placed at least one big order, each customer once, ordered by `customer_id`.
hints_md: You only need to know whether a customer has at least one qualifying order, not how many.
Hollis and Kerry each have two big orders. How many rows should each of them contribute to the result?
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Semi-join, 'rows in A that have at least one match in B' without multiplying them. Interviewers ask 'customers who ordered X' and watch for duplicates.

**Shape:** filter customers by the existence of a qualifying order, rather than combining both tables row by row.

**Syntax:** `EXISTS (subquery)` is true as soon as one row comes back, and the select list is ignored. `x IN (subquery)` tests membership in the set of returned values. Neither multiplies the outer rows.

**Trap:** a plain JOIN returns one row per matching order, so customers with several big orders repeat. Also check the boundary: 'or more' includes exactly 500.00.

**Interview follow-up:** when would you prefer JOIN with DISTINCT over EXISTS, and what does it cost?

solutions.label: EXISTS
solutions.explain_md: Each customer is kept once if at least one big order refers to them, however many there are.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.total >= 500
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

solutions.label: IN
solutions.explain_md: Membership in the set of customers who have a big order; a set has no duplicates to multiply the rows.
solutions.sql:
SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total >= 500)
ORDER BY customer_id;

traps.explain_md: A plain join returns one row per big order, so Hollis and Kerry each appear twice.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.total >= 500
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

traps.explain_md: A strict `>` leaves out Imani, whose only big order is exactly 500.00.
traps.sql:
SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 500)
ORDER BY customer_id;

problems.title: Listeners who played both genres
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: A Spotify-style music service plans a crossover playlist and needs every user who has played at least one Jazz track and at least one Lo-fi track (they may have played other genres too). Return `user_id` and `display_name`, one row per user, ordered by `user_id`.

tables.name: track_plays
tables.description_md: One row per track played by a user.

hints_md: Each play is its own row, so one row can never be both a Jazz row and a Lo-fi row. You have to combine information from several rows of the same user.
Some users played the same genre several times. Count what you need carefully.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** 'Has all of these' (a small relational-division problem). Interviewers phrase it as 'users who did A and B' and wait for the single-row mistake.

**Shape:** either check, for each required genre, that the user has a play of that genre, or group the user's qualifying plays and require that the number of distinct genres equals the number required.

**Syntax:** `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts different values, ignoring repeats; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation, `WHERE` filters rows before it; `col IN ('A', 'B')` is shorthand for an OR of equalities.

**Trap:** requiring one row to equal two different values returns nothing; and counting rows instead of distinct genres lets repeat plays of one genre stand in for the second.

**Interview follow-up:** how would the query change for users who played Jazz but never Lo-fi?

solutions.label: Group and count distinct genres
solutions.explain_md: Restrict to the two genres, group per user, and require both distinct genres to be present. Repeat plays do not count twice.
solutions.sql:
SELECT u.user_id, u.display_name
FROM users u
JOIN track_plays p ON p.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE p.genre IN ('Jazz', 'Lo-fi')
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.display_name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.genre) = 2
ORDER BY u.user_id;

solutions.label: Two EXISTS tests
solutions.explain_md: One existence test per required genre, combined with AND.
solutions.sql:
SELECT u.user_id, u.display_name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM track_plays p WHERE p.user_id = u.user_id AND p.genre = 'Jazz')
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM track_plays p WHERE p.user_id = u.user_id AND p.genre = 'Lo-fi')
ORDER BY u.user_id;

traps.explain_md: A single play row has one genre, so it cannot equal both values; the result is empty.
traps.sql:
SELECT u.user_id, u.display_name
FROM users u
JOIN track_plays p ON p.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE p.genre = 'Jazz' AND p.genre = 'Lo-fi'
ORDER BY u.user_id;

traps.explain_md: Counting rows instead of distinct genres accepts Sam (two Jazz plays) and rejects Vik (one Jazz and two Lo-fi plays).
traps.sql:
SELECT u.user_id, u.display_name
FROM users u
JOIN track_plays p ON p.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE p.genre IN ('Jazz', 'Lo-fi')
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.display_name
HAVING COUNT(*) = 2
ORDER BY u.user_id;

problems.title: Rank tier for every player
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: An online game shows each player's rank tier, which depends on their rating according to the `rank_tiers` table. Return `player_id`, `handle`, `rating` and `tier`, ordered by `player_id`. A player who has not finished placement matches has a NULL rating and should still be listed, with a NULL tier.

tables.name: players
tables.description_md: One row per player. `rating` is NULL until placement matches are finished.

tables.name: rank_tiers
tables.description_md: Inclusive rating ranges: a rating belongs to a tier when it lies between `min_rating` and `max_rating`, both ends included.

hints_md: The two tables share no common column. What relationship between a rating and a tier's limits connects them?
Ratings such as 2500, 2499, 1000 and 0 sit exactly on tier limits. Check where each of them lands.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Range join (non-equi join) to a lookup table of bands. Interviewers use it for grades, tax brackets, age groups, rank tiers.

**Shape:** match each rating to the tier whose limits contain it, keeping players that match nothing.

**Syntax:** `x BETWEEN lo AND hi` is the same as `x >= lo AND x <= hi` (both ends included). A join condition does not have to be an equality; any boolean expression works in `ON`.

**Trap:** a half-open or one-sided condition: using only the lower limit matches a rating to every tier beneath it, and a strict comparison drops ratings that sit on a limit.

**Interview follow-up:** what happens if two tiers overlap, and how would you catch it?

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN with BETWEEN
solutions.explain_md: The rating is joined to the tier that contains it; LEFT JOIN keeps the player whose NULL rating matches no tier.
solutions.sql:
SELECT p.player_id, p.handle, p.rating, t.tier
FROM players p
LEFT JOIN rank_tiers t ON p.rating BETWEEN t.min_rating AND t.max_rating
ORDER BY p.player_id;

solutions.label: Scalar subquery
solutions.explain_md: Looks up the matching tier for each player; no match gives NULL.
solutions.sql:
SELECT p.player_id, p.handle, p.rating,
       (SELECT t.tier FROM rank_tiers t
        WHERE p.rating BETWEEN t.min_rating AND t.max_rating) AS tier
FROM players p
ORDER BY p.player_id;

traps.explain_md: Only checking the lower limit matches a rating to every tier whose minimum it reaches, so most players get several rows.
traps.sql:
SELECT p.player_id, p.handle, p.rating, t.tier
FROM players p
LEFT JOIN rank_tiers t ON p.rating >= t.min_rating
ORDER BY p.player_id, t.tier;

traps.explain_md: Making the lower limit strict loses every rating that sits exactly on a minimum (2500, 2000, 1500, 1000, 0) - they get a NULL tier.
traps.sql:
SELECT p.player_id, p.handle, p.rating, t.tier
FROM players p
LEFT JOIN rank_tiers t ON p.rating > t.min_rating AND p.rating <= t.max_rating
ORDER BY p.player_id;

problems.title: Rate in force on the ride date
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: An Uber-style ride-hailing company changes its per-kilometre rate by city over time. `rate_card` records every rate with the first and last day it applied; the rate still in force has no end date. For each ride return `ride_id`, `city`, `ride_date`, `rate_per_km` (the rate in force on the ride date) and `fare` (`distance_km * rate_per_km`). Order by `ride_id`.

tables.name: rate_card
tables.description_md: One row per rate period. `valid_from` and `valid_to` are both inclusive days; `valid_to` is NULL for the current rate.

hints_md: Each ride should match exactly one rate row of its city. Which two dates in `rate_card` bracket the ride date?
What does a NULL `valid_to` mean, and what does a comparison with NULL do?
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Range join to a history table (slowly changing dimension / effective dating). Interviewers ask for 'the value as of a date'.

**Shape:** match on the city, then require the ride date to fall inside the rate period; the open-ended period needs its own treatment.

**Syntax:** `d BETWEEN a AND b` is inclusive on both ends and is unknown when `b` is NULL. `COALESCE(x, fallback)` replaces a NULL with a stand-in value; `IS NULL` is the only reliable NULL test.

**Trap:** joining to the current rate only, or a BETWEEN that silently discards the open-ended row.

**Interview follow-up:** how would you stop two overlapping rate periods from double-counting a ride?

solutions.label: Range join with an open end
solutions.explain_md: The ride matches the period that started on or before the date and has not ended before it; NULL `valid_to` means still open.
solutions.sql:
SELECT r.ride_id, r.city, r.ride_date, c.rate_per_km,
       r.distance_km * c.rate_per_km AS fare
FROM rides r
JOIN rate_card c
  ON c.city = r.city
 AND r.ride_date >= c.valid_from
 AND (c.valid_to IS NULL OR r.ride_date <= c.valid_to)
ORDER BY r.ride_id;

solutions.label: Latest rate started on or before the date
solutions.explain_md: Pick the rate period with the greatest start date that is not after the ride date; no end date is needed.
solutions.sql:
SELECT r.ride_id, r.city, r.ride_date, c.rate_per_km,
       r.distance_km * c.rate_per_km AS fare
FROM rides r
JOIN rate_card c
  ON c.city = r.city
 AND c.valid_from = (
       SELECT MAX(c2.valid_from) FROM rate_card c2
       WHERE c2.city = r.city AND c2.valid_from <= r.ride_date)
ORDER BY r.ride_id;

traps.explain_md: Always using the current rate rewrites history: older rides are charged today's rate.
traps.sql:
SELECT r.ride_id, r.city, r.ride_date, c.rate_per_km,
       r.distance_km * c.rate_per_km AS fare
FROM rides r
JOIN rate_card c ON c.city = r.city AND c.valid_to IS NULL
ORDER BY r.ride_id;

traps.explain_md: BETWEEN is unknown when `valid_to` is NULL, so every ride taken under a still-current rate disappears.
traps.sql:
SELECT r.ride_id, r.city, r.ride_date, c.rate_per_km,
       r.distance_km * c.rate_per_km AS fare
FROM rides r
JOIN rate_card c
  ON c.city = r.city
 AND r.ride_date BETWEEN c.valid_from AND c.valid_to
ORDER BY r.ride_id;

problems.title: Double-booked calendars
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: An Outlook-style calendar export lists every event with its owner and time range. Return every pair of events belonging to the same owner whose time ranges overlap, as `owner`, `event_a` and `event_b`, where `event_a` is the smaller `event_id`. An event that ends exactly when another starts is not a conflict. Each pair appears once; order by `owner`, `event_a`, `event_b`.

tables.name: calendar_events
tables.description_md: One row per calendar event. `ends_at` is the moment the event is over.

hints_md: Two time ranges overlap when each one starts before the other one ends. Test it on a pair where one event sits completely inside another.
Look at the calendars of maya and owen: some events touch end-to-start, and a lower `event_id` does not always start earlier.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Interval overlap via a self-join. Interviewers ask for 'conflicting bookings', 'overlapping shifts', 'concurrent sessions'.

**Shape:** pair events of the same owner, keep each pair in one orientation, and apply the overlap test that holds for every arrangement (partial overlap, containment, identical ranges).

**Syntax:** an overlap test is two comparisons joined by AND, each comparing one range's start with the other range's end; use strict `<` when touching ends must not count. `a.id < b.id` yields each unordered pair once.

**Trap:** only testing whether the second event starts inside the first misses pairs where the second starts earlier; non-strict comparisons turn back-to-back events into conflicts.

**Interview follow-up:** how would you find the maximum number of events running at the same time for one owner instead?

solutions.label: Self-join with the two-sided overlap test
solutions.explain_md: Two ranges overlap exactly when each starts before the other ends. Strict comparisons treat an event that ends at 10:00 and one that starts at 10:00 as compatible, and the id condition lists each pair once.
solutions.sql:
SELECT a.owner, a.event_id AS event_a, b.event_id AS event_b
FROM calendar_events a
JOIN calendar_events b
  ON a.owner = b.owner
 AND a.event_id < b.event_id
 AND a.starts_at < b.ends_at
 AND b.starts_at < a.ends_at
ORDER BY a.owner, a.event_id, b.event_id;

traps.explain_md: Non-strict comparisons make back-to-back events (09:00-10:00 then 10:00-11:00) count as conflicts.
traps.sql:
SELECT a.owner, a.event_id AS event_a, b.event_id AS event_b
FROM calendar_events a
JOIN calendar_events b
  ON a.owner = b.owner
 AND a.event_id < b.event_id
 AND a.starts_at <= b.ends_at
 AND b.starts_at <= a.ends_at
ORDER BY a.owner, a.event_id, b.event_id;

traps.explain_md: Checking only that the later-numbered event starts inside the earlier one misses pairs in which the higher id starts before the lower id.
traps.sql:
SELECT a.owner, a.event_id AS event_a, b.event_id AS event_b
FROM calendar_events a
JOIN calendar_events b
  ON a.owner = b.owner
 AND a.event_id < b.event_id
 AND b.starts_at >= a.starts_at
 AND b.starts_at < a.ends_at
ORDER BY a.owner, a.event_id, b.event_id;

problems.title: Mutual connections
problems.section: Joins: self, anti, semi and range
problems.statement_md: A LinkedIn-style network stores each connection once, as `member_a` and `member_b` with `member_a < member_b`; a connection works in both directions. For every connection return `member_a`, `member_b` and `mutual_connections`, the number of other members connected to both of them (0 if none). Order by `member_a`, `member_b`.

tables.name: connections
tables.description_md: One row per connection, stored once with `member_a < member_b`.

hints_md: A connection stored as (1, 2) also means 2 is connected to 1, but the table only lists one direction. What would make both directions visible to a join?
Connections with no mutual connection must still appear, with a count of 0.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern:** Graph neighbours with a self-join ('friends of friends', 'common connections'). Interviewers use it to test whether you notice that stored-once pairs need symmetrising.

**Shape:** first build a list of directed links that contains both directions of every connection; then, for each connection, find members linked to both people and count them, keeping connections with none.

**Syntax:** `UNION ALL` appends the rows of a second query to the first and keeps duplicates (`UNION` removes them). `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values, so on an outer-joined column it counts only real matches while `COUNT(*)` counts the unmatched row too.

**Trap:** using the table as stored sees only half the links, so a mutual connection with a smaller or larger id than both people is missed; inner joins drop connections with zero mutual ones.

**Interview follow-up:** how would you suggest new connections: people with the most mutual connections who are not yet connected?

solutions.label: Symmetrise, then join twice
solutions.explain_md: The CTE lists every link in both directions. For each connection, one join finds the contacts of member_a and a second finds those of member_b with the same other member; COUNT on the second side counts real matches only.
solutions.sql:
WITH links AS (
  SELECT member_a AS u, member_b AS v FROM connections
  UNION ALL
  SELECT member_b, member_a FROM connections
)
SELECT c.member_a, c.member_b, COUNT(l2.v) AS mutual_connections
FROM connections c
LEFT JOIN links l1 ON l1.u = c.member_a
LEFT JOIN links l2 ON l2.u = c.member_b AND l2.v = l1.v
GROUP BY c.member_a, c.member_b
ORDER BY c.member_a, c.member_b;

solutions.label: Correlated count over the symmetric list
solutions.explain_md: For each connection, count the members that appear as a neighbour of both people.
solutions.sql:
WITH links AS (
  SELECT member_a AS u, member_b AS v FROM connections
  UNION ALL
  SELECT member_b, member_a FROM connections
)
SELECT c.member_a, c.member_b,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
        FROM links x JOIN links y ON y.v = x.v
        WHERE x.u = c.member_a AND y.u = c.member_b) AS mutual_connections
FROM connections c
ORDER BY c.member_a, c.member_b;

traps.explain_md: Without symmetrising, only mutual connections whose id is larger than both people are found, and connections with none disappear.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.member_a, c.member_b, COUNT(*) AS mutual_connections
FROM connections c
JOIN connections x ON x.member_a = c.member_a
JOIN connections y ON y.member_a = c.member_b AND y.member_b = x.member_b
GROUP BY c.member_a, c.member_b
ORDER BY c.member_a, c.member_b;

traps.explain_md: Symmetrised but with inner joins: connections that have no mutual connection vanish instead of showing 0.
traps.sql:
WITH links AS (
  SELECT member_a AS u, member_b AS v FROM connections
  UNION ALL
  SELECT member_b, member_a FROM connections
)
SELECT c.member_a, c.member_b, COUNT(*) AS mutual_connections
FROM connections c
JOIN links l1 ON l1.u = c.member_a
JOIN links l2 ON l2.u = c.member_b AND l2.v = l1.v
GROUP BY c.member_a, c.member_b
ORDER BY c.member_a, c.member_b;
